SECTION 1 OF 7 · SPOT THE HAZARD

Safety = the measures and practices that protect life, health and environment.

Today you practise, not read: spot hazards, run a Code Red drill, pick the right extinguisher, triage a spill and read a chemical register.

Noor: Safety is the habits that protect life, health and environment. Today you practise them. Keep the main point connected to a familiar task or conversation. That connection makes the information easier to use when it matters. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear.

Teach risk scoring

Problem: it is raining and the floor at the clinic entrance is wet. Score the risk as likelihood × impact (consequence), each on a 1–5 scale.

  1. 1Step 1
    Name the hazard: wet floor at a busy entrance.
    A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm to people, property or environment. Name it before you score it.
  2. 2Step 2
    Likelihood = 4 (busy entrance, rain all afternoon).
    Likelihood asks how probable harm is. Many people cross a wet surface, so a slip is likely.
  3. 3Step 3
    Impact = 3 (a fall can cause injury).
    Impact asks how bad the harm would be. It is scored separately from likelihood because a rare event can still be severe.
  4. 4Step 4
    Risk = 4 × 3 = 12.
    Multiplying the two scores ranks this risk against others so you know what to fix first.
  5. 5Step 5
    Control: entrance mat + wet-floor sign + a mop schedule.
    Each control lowers a different part of the score: the mat and mopping cut likelihood; the sign warns people while the floor is still wet.

Why is the sign not enough on its own? This reflection is not scored.

Not graded
Noor: Walk through the wet-floor example aloud. Explain why likelihood and impact are scored separately. Follow the example one step at a time, then identify why the next step makes sense. The value is the reasoning you can carry into a similar case. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Find the hazards

Six hazards are hidden in this store room. Open all six markers to see the hazard and its control.

Noor's tip: “I walked past a blocked exit for a week before I noticed it.”

0/6

Select a region to see its details.

Standing on a wheeled chair

A chair with wheels can roll away and cause a fall from height. Control: use an approved step stool or kick step, and store heavy items lower.

Trailing cables across the walkway

Cables across a walkway are a trip hazard and get damaged underfoot. Control: reroute along the wall, use a cable cover, or report for a new socket.

Blocked fire exit and extinguisher

Boxes in front of the exit and extinguisher slow everyone's escape and hide the equipment. Control: clear the exit now and keep the area marked and free at all times.

Boxes stacked above shoulder height

High stacks can fall and cause strain injuries when lifted down. Control: heavy items on low shelves, keep stacks below shoulder height.

Unlabelled bottle on a shelf

Nobody can tell what is inside, what it does or how to clean it up. Control: do not use it; label it from the register and SDS, or remove it through EHS.

Liquid spill near a socket

Liquid next to electricity is a shock and slip hazard. Control: keep people away, do not touch the plug with wet hands, report it and clean the spill safely.

Noor: Set up the store room. There are six hazards. Open them all. I walked past a blocked exit for a week before I noticed it. Let each marker add context rather than rushing to a conclusion.

Prioritise

You found six hazards in the store room. Which one do you report and fix first?

Right. A blocked exit has a severe impact on everyone in the building if a fire starts, so it ranks highest.

A real trip hazard with a high likelihood, but the impact is usually one person's fall. The blocked exit could affect everyone.

Important to fix, but the likelihood of harm right now is low while nobody uses it. A blocked exit affects everyone in an emergency.

Stop them, yes, but that's one person and one moment. The blocked exit is a standing risk for the whole building.

Code Red drill

Noor · Safety liaison

Code Red drill. A weekday afternoon in the clinic. Smoke is coming from Consultation Room 3 on the first floor.

Six decisions, one for each moment of the response. You have 2 lives and one text hint per decision. There is no timer here, but in real life seconds matter. Pass: at least 5 of 6 right.

Code wording and extension ⚠ Draft — pending D2. Assembly-point names ⚠ Draft — pending B8.

Score: 0♥ 0⏱ 0

1 · Rescue. You open the door of Consultation Room 3. Smoke is gathering under the ceiling and the patient is still in the chair. What do you do first?

  • Right. R — Rescue: anyone in immediate danger comes first. The alarm follows straight after.

  • Poster rule: RACE starts with Rescue — move anyone in immediate danger before you go to the phone. The patient was left in a smoke-filled room. You lose a life.

  • Poster rule: Rescue first. Investigating the source while a patient breathes smoke wastes the seconds that matter. You lose a life.

2 · Alarm. The patient is safe in the corridor. You shout “Code Red!” and pull the call point. Dr. Omar comes out of the next room: “I'll call it in. What exactly do I say?”

He dials the clinic emergency extension (⚠ Draft — pending D2). Which script is complete?

  • Right. A — Alarm: shout “Code Red”, activate the call point, then call and state the code type, location, and your ID and name. All three are here.

  • Poster rule: the call must give the code type, location, and your ID and name. This script gives none of them, so the team doesn't know where to go. You lose a life.

  • Poster rule: code type, exact location, ID and name. “First floor” is not a location the team can go straight to, and nobody knows who called. You lose a life.

3 · Contain. The room has an oxygen cylinder, an alcohol rub dispenser and the patient's paper file. What do you do before you leave?

  • Right. C — Contain: remove oxygen cylinders and alcohol-based sanitiser, which feed a fire, and close the room's door to hold back smoke.

  • Poster rule: close the room's doors. An open door lets smoke and fire spread down the corridor. The file is not a fire hazard to remove. You lose a life.

  • Poster rule: remove the oxygen cylinders and alcohol rub — they feed the fire. The file can wait; the oxygen can't. You lose a life.

4 · Extinguish or evacuate? The picture shows two ways this could look: a small fire inside the metal waste bin, or flames climbing the curtain into the ceiling. Which rule do you follow?

  • Right. E — Extinguish / Evacuate: extinguish small fires only if you are trained to do so. A spreading fire means you leave and evacuate.

  • Poster rule: extinguish small fires only, and only if trained. A spreading fire is an evacuation. You lose a life.

  • Poster rule: extinguish small fires if trained to do so. Untrained use wastes time and puts you at risk. You lose a life.

5 · Evacuate. Evacuation is called. A patient who uses a wheelchair and cannot walk is on the first floor. How do you get them down?

  • Right. Rescue patients using evacuation tools: the evacuation chair is made for stairs.

  • Poster rule: use the evacuation tools — the evacuation chair on the stairs. Elevators can stop or open onto the fire floor during a fire. You lose a life.

  • Poster rule: rescue patients using evacuation tools. An evacuation chair lets two trained staff bring them down the stairs now. You lose a life.

6 · Assembly point. You reach the outside assembly point (⚠ Draft — pending B8) with the patient. The smoke seems to have cleared and some colleagues start walking back in. What do you do?

  • Right. Nobody re-enters until the End of disaster announcement. Reporting in means the team can account for everyone. Announcement wording ⚠ Draft — pending D2.

  • Rule: wait for the all-clear. Smoke clearing doesn't mean the building is safe, and the team needs to count everyone at the assembly point. You lose a life.

  • Rule: stay at the assembly point until the all-clear. If you leave, the team may think you are still inside and search for you. You lose a life.

Drill debrief — RACE

  1. Rescue — the patient out of the smoke first.
  2. Alarm — shout “Code Red”, pull the call point, call: code type, location, ID and name.
  3. Contain — remove O₂ and alcohol rub, close the door.
  4. Extinguish — only a small fire, only if trained (PASS); otherwise evacuate.
  5. Evacuate — evacuation chair on the stairs, never the elevator.
  6. Assembly point — report in and wait for the all-clear.

  • Drill complete. Check your score below.

Assembly points

Two assembly points

Inside assembly point: a safe area inside the building, used in horizontal or vertical evacuation.

Outside assembly point: the signed meeting place outside, used in a full evacuation. Names per branch ⚠ Draft — pending B8.

Three levels of evacuation (recap from module 01)

Horizontal (to the next safe zone on the same floor) → vertical (down to a lower floor) → full (out of the building).

Find your unit's evacuation plan on the wall today.

What is HAZMAT; Code Orange

HAZMAT — any substance or agent that, if released or misused, can pose a threat to the environment, life or health.

Code Orange — a leak or release of hazardous material: a chemical or a biological spill.

One rule decides Code Orange: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team.

⚠ Draft — pending D1: the source deck gives two thresholds (under 1 L “minor” and over 500 mL); this is the recommended single rule.

Noor: HAZMAT is chemical or biological. One clear rule decides Code Orange. Notice which part of the information you would need first in practice. Use that as the starting point for a safe, respectful next action. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task.

Spill triage

Dr. Omar · Family physician

Three spills on one shift. For each, decide the kit and whether to call Code Orange.

The rule: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

Score: 0

A urine sample pot is dropped in the lab corridor and splashes on the floor.

  • Right. A small biological spill, nothing highly toxic: below the threshold, so no Code Orange. Use the yellow biological kit. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • The rule: Code Orange at 500 mL or more, or a highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance. One sample is neither. Use the biological kit. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • No Code Orange is needed, but body fluids still need the biological kit and PPE, not bare paper towels.

A one-litre container of surface disinfectant tips over in the store. Most of it is on the floor.

  • Right. Well over 500 mL of a chemical is above the threshold: Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • The rule is about volume as well as toxicity: 500 mL or more means Code Orange, whatever the product. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • The cleaning supervisor handles spills below the threshold. This one is above 500 mL: Code Orange, and nobody leaves it. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

A few drops of a reagent labelled “highly toxic” leak from a cracked vial in the lab.

  • Right. Any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance means Code Orange, regardless of volume. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • Volume isn't the only test: any highly toxic substance means Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • This is a chemical, and a highly toxic one: Code Orange, regardless of volume. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

Spill-kit procedure

Put the chemical spill-kit procedure in order. Procedure ⚠ Draft — pending B4 (EHS writes the final steps).

  1. Put on PPE as the SDS requires
  2. Isolate the area and warn others
  3. Contain the edges of the spill
  4. Absorb or neutralise
  5. Bag, seal and label as hazardous waste
  6. Clean the area and report to your supervisor and Safety Services
  7. Restock the kit

SDS column: ✓ means the Safety Data Sheet is on file. ✘ means do not use the product until the SDS is supplied: report it to your supervisor or EHS.

NFPA column: Health (blue) · Flammability (red) · Reactivity (yellow) · Special (white), each 0–4. 4 = can be lethal / extremely flammable / may detonate; 0 = normal / will not burn / stable.

Register decision

Register row 4: Surface disinfectant X — SDS ✘.

You need it for a cleaning task right now. What do you do?

Right. Without the SDS nobody can confirm the hazards, the PPE or the spill response. Use another product with an SDS on file.

The label is a summary. The SDS tells you the PPE, first aid and spill response. No SDS, no use.

Gloves may not be the right PPE, and you can't know without the SDS. Report first, and don't use it until the SDS is on file.

A similar product's SDS may not match this one. The register needs the SDS for this exact product.

NFPA in practice

Register row 3: Solvent (isopropyl alcohol 70%), NFPA 2-3-0 (health 2 · flammability 3 · reactivity 0).

Where must it be stored?

Right. Flammability 3 means it ignites easily at normal temperatures, so it belongs in the self-closing flammable cabinet, away from heat and ignition sources.

A label doesn't stop vapour reaching a heat source. Flammability 3 needs the flammable cabinet.

A domestic fridge has ignition sources inside and is never for chemicals. Use the flammable cabinet.

Mixed storage and no fire protection. Flammability 3 means the approved flammable cabinet.
